recoveryRoadmap.description: General family recovery checklist after a death. Registration, estate, tax, and benefit processes vary by province or territory; confirm current requirements with the relevant authority.

meta.title: Family Recovery Roadmap – Canada
meta.reviewedBy: Federal sources reviewed; province- and territory-specific legal review remains necessary

intro.condolence: We are sorry for your loss. This roadmap is meant to reduce confusion by showing what matters first and what can wait.
intro.howToUse: Begin with immediate records and financial access. Then move to insurance, pensions, estate administration, and long-term family protection.

startHere.0: Follow the province or territory's death-registration process and ask which death records or certificates are needed.
startHere.1: List regular bills and contact providers before stopping payments or automatic transfers; confirm account authority and due dates.
startHere.2: Review beneficiaries on life insurance, registered plans, and pensions; confirm ownership and joint-account terms with each institution.
startHere.3: Notify the employer, financial institutions, insurer, executor, and next of kin about the death.
startHere.4: Collect the will, trust records, ID, and insurance policies in a secure place.
startHere.5: Check whether a power of attorney, healthcare directive, or personal representative has been named.
startHere.6: Keep a simple log of every call, claim, and appointment.

legalFramework.0: Provincial and territorial estate administration, probate, and succession law
legalFramework.1: Quebec civil law and Quebec-specific will, mandate, and estate procedures
legalFramework.3: CPP and OAS survivor benefit rules
legalFramework.4: RRSP, TFSA, and retirement plan beneficiary rules
legalFramework.5: Provincial tenancy and property transfer rules
legalFramework.6: Provincial, territorial, and federal tax filing requirements for a deceased estate

0.title: Immediate stabilization
0.focus: Secure documents, money, and critical records before family and legal tasks expand.

0.action: Ask the vital-statistics authority and each institution what death record or certificate format it requires; order the appropriate copies.
0.why: Document requirements and available certificate types vary by province or territory and by institution.
0.legalRef: Provincial vital statistics and registration rules

1.action: Review ownership and beneficiary or successor-holder designations on joint accounts, registered plans, pensions, and insurance. Confirm the treatment of each asset with the institution and a local professional.
1.why: Ownership, designation, and estate rules vary by asset and province or territory; do not assume an asset passes directly to another person.

2.action: Identify recurring bills and speak with each provider before stopping payments. Confirm who is responsible, what remains due, and how to avoid missed essential services.
2.why: Automatic cancellations or payments from a restricted account can create service, credit, or legal problems.

3.action: Arrange a secure place for original documents and records: passport, SIN, health card, insurance policies, will, powers of attorney, deeds, and tax filings.
3.why: Each bank, insurer, and court sets its own acceptable-document requirements; keep originals secure and ask before sending them.
3.legalRef: Document retention and estate administration practice

4.action: Tell the employer or pension administrator about the death and ask about final pay, pension death benefits, severance, or group insurance coverage.
4.why: Employer plans often have separate rules and deadlines from personal insurance products.
4.legalRef: Federal pension and employer benefit rules

5.action: Contact all insurers to begin life insurance, health insurance, mortgage, or funeral benefit claims. Ask whether the claim is being reviewed under a contestability or investigation process.
5.why: Insurance benefits and policy continuation can matter for costs, debt payment, and family cash flow.
5.legalRef: Insurance contract terms and provincial/federal insurance rules

6.action: Review whether a will, trust, or personal representative has been appointed. Ask for a copy of the estate documents and understand who has authority to act.
6.why: A clear chain of authority reduces friction and helps avoid disputes about who can access funds or records.

criticalMistakes.0: Ordering the wrong certificate type or assuming every institution accepts the same document.
criticalMistakes.1: Assuming every account will go through probate. Beneficiaries and joint accounts may work differently.
criticalMistakes.2: Paying debts before checking whether an insurer or policy covers them.
criticalMistakes.3: Using the deceased person's online banking or card after death without authority.
criticalMistakes.4: Ignoring the will, trust, or healthcare directive because the family believes it is not urgent.
criticalMistakes.5: Waiting too long to inform the employer or pension administrator about the death.

0.deadline: As soon as possible under provincial rules
0.consequence: Delays can slow down bank, insurer, and probate steps.

1.deadline: Follow the employer or plan deadlines immediately
1.consequence: Benefits may be delayed or lost if filed late.

2.deadline: Usually a matter of weeks once all documents are available
2.consequence: The family may struggle with daily costs while waiting for payment.

1.title: Claims and account transfer
1.focus: File benefits, move assets, and identify what is probate and what is not.

0.action: File life insurance, pension, CPP survivor, OAS survivor, and any employer death benefits. Include the death certificate, beneficiary details, and policy or account numbers.
0.why: These benefits often move outside the estate and should be filed early to support household cash flow.
0.legalRef: Federal pension, insurance, and employer benefit rules

1.action: Transfer or close bank, RRSP, TFSA, brokerage, and savings accounts according to the account terms and beneficiary instructions.
1.why: Some accounts require an estate process before they can transfer, and others pass directly to the named beneficiary.

2.action: Review vehicles, property, and titled assets. Confirm whether the title or deed requires a transfer form, probate process, or land/vehicle office filing.
2.why: This prevents delays when family members later need to sell, insure, or use the asset.
2.legalRef: Provincial property and title transfer law

3.action: Check all loans, credit cards, and mortgages and ask each lender whether death benefits or insurance covers the balance.
3.why: Do not pay debt blindly when a policy or benefit may already be available.

4.action: Open or confirm the estate administration process if assets require probate or a personal representative. The executor may need to file court documents and maintain a record of all assets and debts.
4.why: Estate administration can protect the family and make it clear who is acting under the law.
4.legalRef: Provincial estate administration and probate procedures

5.action: Keep a ledger of what has been paid out, what is still owing, and which documents are needed for each account and asset. This is especially important for mixed assets and family property.
5.why: A clean record prevents confusion and helps with later tax or family discussions.

mustHaveDocuments.2: Bank, RRSP, TFSA, and brokerage information
mustHaveDocuments.3: Vehicle title and real estate deeds
mustHaveDocuments.4: Loan, mortgage, and credit card records
mustHaveDocuments.5: Will, trust papers, and probate documents
mustHaveDocuments.7: List of estate assets and liabilities

criticalMistakes.0: Failing to file all benefits before the family feels the cash squeeze.
criticalMistakes.1: Assuming that all property will transfer automatically or without title steps.
criticalMistakes.2: Not checking whether the bank or financial institution requires a beneficiary or personal representative filing.
criticalMistakes.3: Allowing a probate or transfer issue to sit unresolved while the family tries to sell or insure property.
criticalMistakes.4: Ignoring pension, RRSP, and TFSA beneficiary designations.
criticalMistakes.5: Paying family or estate debts without checking the available insurance or benefit coverage.

0.deadline: File promptly once the documents are available
0.consequence: Late filing can create stress, delays, and missed deadlines for cash support.

1.deadline: No single universal deadline, but file promptly when court action is needed
1.consequence: Delays can increase legal cost and uncertainty.

2.deadline: Follow federal and provincial deadlines for the deceased and the estate
2.consequence: Missing tax filings can create penalties and interest.

2.title: Legal and financial settlement
2.focus: Complete estate administration, taxes, property transfer, and debt handling.

0.action: If probate or estate administration is required, maintain a complete file of assets, liabilities, dates, and communications. This is the estate record the family will rely on.
0.why: Good records reduce disputes and make later reporting simpler.

1.action: File the deceased's final tax return and review all necessary estate filings. Ask whether a personal representative or executor has filing obligations.
1.why: Tax obligations may continue after death and may involve the estate if money or property is still being managed.

2.action: Review mortgages, lines of credit, car loans, credit cards, and other debt. Confirm whether any policy or benefit pays a balance or protects the family from a debt burden.
2.why: Some debt is personal, some is estate debt, and some is covered by insurance or benefits.

3.action: Complete property transfers, utility changes, vehicle update, and lien or title review before selling or transferring real estate.
3.why: Title issues and liens can block a sale or create family conflict if not corrected early.

4.action: Review the will, trust, healthcare directives, and any powers of attorney. Ask whether the family needs to change account authority or appoint a new representative.
4.why: Authority changes often matter just as much as asset transfers.

5.action: Inventory important email, cloud, financial, social, and subscription accounts. Use each provider's official legacy or bereavement process and keep credentials in a separate password manager.
5.why: Digital access is frequently overlooked and can hide dollars, communication records, or important documents.
5.legalRef: Provider terms, privacy rules, and estate authority

mustHaveDocuments.2: Final tax return and estate filing records
mustHaveDocuments.3: Mortgage, deed, lien, and title documents
mustHaveDocuments.6: Digital account inventory and authorized recovery-plan location; do not include passwords or recovery codes

criticalMistakes.0: Confusing the estate process with beneficiary transfer. The steps differ depending on the asset.
criticalMistakes.1: Failing to file the final tax return or to keep a list of unpaid liabilities.
criticalMistakes.2: Selling or transferring property before title, mortgage, and lien checks are complete.
criticalMistakes.3: Ignoring a trust or directive because the family believes a will is enough.
criticalMistakes.4: Leaving digital accounts unmanaged after a death.
criticalMistakes.5: Paying debts without checking whether insurance or benefits cover them.

0.deadline: Follow federal and provincial deadlines for the deceased and estate
0.consequence: Late filing can create penalties and unnecessary stress.

1.deadline: As soon as practical when court procedures are required
1.consequence: Delay can increase cost and family conflict.

2.deadline: Complete before sale or refinancing if the asset is being transferred
2.consequence: A title issue can block a sale or create a legal dispute.

3.title: Rebuild and protect the family
3.focus: Update plans, beneficiaries, and emergency records so the family is not exposed to the same risks again.

0.action: Review and update beneficiary designations on all bank, retirement, life, and investment accounts. Keep a copy of the confirmation for each account.
0.why: This is one of the cleanest ways to reduce future delays and confusion.
0.legalRef: Financial account and insurance beneficiary rules

1.action: Review the will, trust, powers of attorney, and healthcare directives. Update these after major life events, including marriage, divorce, new children, or a move.
1.why: A family plan needs to reflect the current situation, not just the last version written years earlier.

2.action: Review the household's accessible cash reserve against its essential expenses, income stability, insurance, and available support.
2.why: An appropriate reserve depends on household needs, obligations, and available benefits; avoid a one-size-fits-all target.

3.action: Review life, health, disability, and mortgage protection coverage. Confirm that the surviving family members still have adequate income replacement and healthcare protection.
3.why: Coverage gaps can appear after a major loss or a job change and can be expensive to fix later.

4.action: Create a family asset register with provider names, useful account references, document locations, and emergency contacts. Keep passwords and recovery codes in a password manager with an appropriate emergency-access feature.
4.why: This creates a practical map that can save time and reduce confusion when a family crisis hits again.
4.legalRef: Recordkeeping and estate planning best practice

5.action: Review all key fiduciary roles, including executor, trustee, power of attorney, and healthcare proxy. Make sure the named person is still the right fit.
5.why: The family should not discover after a crisis that the right legal role is outdated or unclear.

mustHaveDocuments.4: Healthcare directives and powers of attorney

criticalMistakes.1: Leaving executor and fiduciary roles undefined or outdated.
criticalMistakes.2: Failing to review insurance and healthcare coverage after a loss.
criticalMistakes.3: Keeping all estate records in one place with no trusted backup person.
criticalMistakes.4: Not creating a cash reserve before a future emergency hits.
criticalMistakes.5: Assuming legal documents never need to be revisited.

0.consequence: Outdated designations can create family conflict and legal delay.

2.deadline: After marriage, divorce, children, or any significant property change
2.consequence: A stale plan can no longer reflect the family’s needs or wishes.

0.definition: The person named to carry out the terms of the will and handle the estate process.

1.definition: The person appointed to administer the estate under provincial law.

2.definition: The person or entity named to receive an asset or benefit on death.

3.definition: A court or administrative process that may grant authority to administer an estate; the name and requirements vary by province or territory.

4.definition: A legal arrangement that holds assets for the benefit of one or more people.

5.definition: A document authorizing another person to act for you for legal or financial matters.

6.definition: A document outlining healthcare preferences and who can make decisions if you cannot.

7.definition: An account with two or more owners, which may pass to a surviving owner depending on the account type and province.

8.definition: A designation recorded with some insurance, pension, or registered-plan providers. Its effect depends on the asset, contract, and applicable provincial or territorial law.

9.definition: A legal claim on property to secure a debt or obligation.
